opus-5.5.text:
I think world models are going to become one of the most important pieces, but probably not in the way people first imagined.

Right now most VLA models, vision-language-action models, are basically reactive policies. You give them an image and an instruction, and they output an action. They inherit a lot of semantic knowledge from the vision-language pretraining. They know what a cup is, what "put it in the sink" means. But they don't have a very good sense of physics or consequences. They don't really ask, "If I push this here, what happens next?"

A world model fills that gap. It's a model that predicts how the world evolves given an action. Once you have that, there are a few ways it fits into the architecture.

The first is as a training signal or a data engine. Real robot data is extremely expensive. We collect it with teleoperation, one episode at a time, and it doesn't scale like internet text or video. If you have a good world model, a learned simulator really, you can generate a lot of experience, evaluate policies, and even do reinforcement learning inside the model without breaking real hardware. To me that's probably the most immediate value.

The second is as part of the policy itself, for planning. The VLA proposes a few candidate actions, the world model imagines the outcomes, and you pick the one that best achieves the goal. That's closer to how humans handle unfamiliar or delicate tasks. We imagine before we act.

The third, which I find most interesting, is that predicting the future may simply be a better pretraining objective for a robot brain. If a model can predict how a video unfolds, it has implicitly learned something about objects, contact, gravity, and cause and effect. Then the action head becomes a relatively thin layer on top of that understanding. So the line between "world model" and "policy" may blur, and you end up with one model that both imagines and acts.

That said, there are real challenges. Video generation models look impressive, but looking plausible isn't the same as being physically accurate. For manipulation, a small error in contact or friction can be the difference between grasping an object and dropping it. And errors compound when you roll the model forward many steps. So I don't think world models will replace real data or classical simulation soon. I see them as complementary: real data to ground things, physics simulation where we can model the world precisely, and learned world models to cover the long tail that's too messy to hand-engineer.

If I had to summarize, VLAs gave robots common sense about *what* to do. World models are how we give them intuition about *what will happen*. Combining the two is, I think, a key step toward general-purpose robots.

r001.rationale: The response describes world models fitting into VLA architectures for training and planning, and says they complement real data and physics simulation.

r002.rationale: It says a world model can imagine outcomes of candidate actions and help select one, but does not specify using a predicted next-frame visual representation to generate the next action.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most interesting open questions in robot learning right now, so let me try to lay out how I see it.

First, a bit of context. Today's VLA models, the vision-language-action models, are essentially large pretrained vision-language backbones with an action head attached. You feed in camera images and a language instruction, and the model directly outputs motor commands. What's remarkable is how much they inherit from internet-scale pretraining: object recognition, semantic understanding, some commonsense about how the world works. That's why a model like RT-2 or Gemini Robotics can generalize to objects and instructions it has never seen in robot data.

But there's a fundamental gap. A VLA, as it's typically trained, is a reactive policy. It maps the current observation to the next action. It doesn't explicitly ask, "if I do this, what will happen next?" Humans do that constantly. Before I pour water into a glass, I have a mental simulation of the water flowing, the glass filling, whether it will overflow. That predictive capability is what a world model provides, and I think it's the missing piece.

So how do they fit together? I see roughly three ways.

The first is world models as a data engine. Real robot data is the bottleneck. It's slow and expensive to collect. If you have a good learned world model, a video-prediction model conditioned on actions, you can generate enormous amounts of plausible interaction data, roll out policies inside it, and use that to train or fine-tune the VLA. It's simulation, but learned from video rather than hand-built with physics engines, so it can cover visual and physical phenomena that are very hard to model analytically, like deformable objects or liquids.

The second is world models for planning and verification at inference time. The VLA proposes an action or an action chunk, the world model imagines the consequence, and you check whether the imagined future actually accomplishes the goal. That gives you something like System 2 reasoning for a robot. You can sample multiple candidate behaviors and pick the one whose predicted outcome looks best. It also gives you a natural safety check, because you can reject actions whose predicted futures look dangerous before executing them.

The third, and the one I find most exciting long term, is a unified model. Instead of a separate policy and a separate predictor, you train one model that predicts both future observations and actions. Prediction of the future becomes a pretraining objective that teaches physics and causality, and action generation sits on top of that understanding. In that view, the world model isn't a module you bolt on. It's the representation the policy is built from.

Now, the honest caveats. Learned video world models are still not very physically accurate. They hallucinate, objects pass through each other, contact dynamics are often wrong. For many manipulation tasks the hard part is precisely the contact-rich moments, and that's where these models are weakest today. There's also the question of compute. Imagining the future at high resolution is expensive, and robots have to act at tens of hertz. So in the near term I expect a hybrid: world models used offline for data generation and evaluation, and used sparingly online for high-level decisions, with the fast reactive VLA handling the low-level control.

But the trend line is clear to me. Video generation models have improved dramatically in the last couple of years, and the moment they become reliable enough to trust as simulators, they will change robotics in the same way that large language pretraining changed NLP. I'd say world models are not a competitor to VLAs. They're what will turn VLAs from reactive imitators into agents that actually understand the consequences of what they do.

r001.rationale: The response describes world models working alongside a separate VLA for data generation and inference-time planning, and says a near-term system would combine them.

r002.rationale: The response says a unified model could predict future observations and actions, but does not clearly say the next action is generated based on a predicted next-frame visual representation.

astra-6.text:
I think world models can provide the predictive component in a VOA architecture. The robot needs to do more than understand what it sees and produce an action. It also needs some way to anticipate: if I take this action, how will the environment change?

A world model could let the robot compare possible actions before executing them. That is particularly useful for tasks that require several steps, where an action that looks reasonable immediately might lead to a difficult situation later.

The challenge is making those predictions useful for control. A model can produce a plausible future observation and still get the physical interaction wrong. For robotics, we care about whether an object moves as expected, whether a grasp succeeds, and whether the robot can recover when its prediction is wrong.

So I see world models and action policies as complementary. The policy proposes actions, the world model helps evaluate their consequences, and feedback from the real environment keeps the system grounded. How tightly those pieces should be integrated is still an open question.

r001.rationale: The response places a world model within a VOA architecture and describes it as complementary to the action policy.

r002.rationale: It says the world model can predict consequences and help evaluate possible actions, but does not say the architecture generates its next action based on a predicted next-frame visual representation.

sol-6.1.text:
I see world models as a complementary piece. A vision-language-action model maps what the robot sees and what you ask it to do into actions. A world model asks a different question: if the robot takes this action, what will happen next?

You can combine them in a few ways. During training, the world model can provide imagined experience so the policy can learn without collecting every interaction on a physical robot. At deployment, the policy can propose actions, and the world model can help evaluate their consequences before executing them.

The challenge is making those predictions useful for control. A prediction can look visually convincing and still get the contact physics wrong. For a robot, whether an object slips or whether a foot lands securely can matter much more than the appearance of the scene.

So I don’t think the world model necessarily needs to predict every pixel. It needs to capture the aspects of the world that matter for the task, and ideally tell us when its predictions are uncertain. Then the policy and the world model can work together, with real-world feedback continually correcting both.

r001.rationale: The response describes world models as a complementary piece that can be combined with a robotics vision-language-action policy.

r002.rationale: The response says a world model can evaluate proposed actions by predicting their consequences, but does not say the architecture generates its next action based on a predicted next-frame visual representation.
